To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the model of Discoursal Analysis developed by Sinclair & Coulthard (SC) (1975) does not adequately account for the complexity of classroom talk.

the use of the Discourse Analysis model developed by Sinclair and Coultard (1975), to analyse classroom talk, does not provide a complete picture of teacher-student dialogue and the co-constructed, improvisational nature of the dialogue.

the teacher’s use of the morality tale is a communicative strategy that enables the co-construction of a polyphonic classroom dialogue, and that this communicative strategy has implications for the way in which we conceptualize the relationship between teacher and student, and the way we conceptualize teacher–student dialogue in the classroom.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the analysis of teacher–student interaction in the classroom.
the communicative practices that teachers and students engage in when interacting in the classroom.
how the teacher’s voice is constructed in classroom talk, and the implications of this for teacher–student interaction.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the study has shown that the use of a polyphonic approach to teacher-student interaction can reveal how the teacher can use a range of communicative resources to incorporate student contributions within the polyphony and thereby create a more inclusive and democratic learning environment.
this article is a great example of how to analyze a piece of classroom discourse.

this article has shown that the analysis of the prosody and rhythm of speech can be an effective tool to analyse the dynamics of teacher–student interaction and to identify the communicative functions of the speech of the teacher and students.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the analysis of classroom talk is not a simple matter of identifying the teacher’s utterances and the student’s responses to these.
we argue for the need to develop an approach to the study of classroom discourse that is sensitive to the polyphonic nature of teacher– student interaction.
the teacher–student interaction in the classroom is not a monologue, but a dialogue.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the teacher–student interaction is not a linear process but a complex and dynamic interaction that is co-constructed and negotiated by the participants.

the teacher–student relationship can be seen as an improvisatory process in which the teacher and the student co-construct a dialogue in which the student’s point of view is valued and incorporated into the teacher’s own.
we can learn a lot about how students learn by paying careful attention to the ways in which they talk with their teachers.
